title: Planting Undetectable Backdoors in Machine Learning Models
claim: a malicious trainer plants a backdoor no efficient observer detects and no one without the key replicates (computational undetectability)
realization: three constructions: signature-checking module beside any model (black-box); random Fourier features drawn to hide a lattice direction (white-box); random ReLU networks hiding a sparse direction (white-box, sparse PCA)

authors: Kalavasis, Karbasi, Oikonomou, Sotiraki, Velegkas, Zampetakis
title: Injecting Undetectable Backdoors in Obfuscated Neural Networks and Language Models
claim: white-box undetectable, non-replicable backdoors in networks released obfuscated, and in LMs
realization: iO for circuits carried to networks; detecting the backdoor would distinguish obfuscations; LM version assumes a steganographic function

authors: Draguns, Gritsevskiy, Motwani, Rogers-Smith, Ladish, Schroeder de Witt
title: Unelicitable Backdoors in Language Models via Cryptographic Transformer Circuits
claim: LM backdoors a defender cannot even trigger (unelicitable, stronger than undetectable)
realization: signature checking and encrypted payload decoding hand-compiled into the transformer forward pass; evidence empirical

title: Statistically Undetectable Backdoors in Deep Neural Networks
claim: statistically undetectable backdoor, even to an unbounded observer with all weights, giving the planter an adversarial example for every input
realization: frozen random first layer sampled to look Gaussian while nearly cancelling a secret direction; trained bi-Lipschitz layers after it; hardness without the key from number balancing and symmetric bounded perceptron (worst-case lattices)

authors: Draguns, Motwani, Douglas, Schroeder de Witt
title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
claim: a model can hide an entire hidden program, not only a misclassification, hard to elicit without a trigger
realization: an encrypted network inside the host weights, decrypted and run on the trigger (abstract only)

title: Cryptographic Backdoor for Neural Networks: Boon and Bane
claim: the GKVZ22 signature backdoor serves as attack and as defence (watermark, authentication, IP tracking)
realization: signature circuit in parallel with image classifiers, post-quantum signatures, measured overhead; empirical

title: Backdoor Defense, Learnability, and Obfuscation
claim: defending against a random-trigger backdoor depends on the class; statistically by VC dimension, computationally strictly between learning and nothing
realization: attacker-defender game; voting defence; iO plus puncturable PRFs make polynomial circuits undefendable; decision trees defendable faster than learnable

title: Oblivious Defense in ML Models: Backdoor Removal without Detection
claim: a backdoor can be removed without being detected
realization: black-box defender repairs each output at run time from queries at related points, when the ground truth is close to Fourier-heavy, linear or low-degree; some structural assumption is proved necessary

title: A Cryptographic Perspective on Mitigation vs. Detection in Machine Learning
claim: mitigation and detection are equivalent defences for classification and separate for generative tasks
realization: learning tasks with built-in cryptographic puzzles, SNARKs and IVC make mitigation cheap and detection impossible (abstract and theorem statement only)

title: Undetectable Watermarks for Language Models
claim: LM outputs carry a watermark no one detects without the key; undetectability can only be computational
realization: keyed PRF replaces sampling randomness once enough empirical entropy accumulates; detection recomputes it; one-way functions suffice

authors: Zhang, Edelman, Francati, Venturi, Ateniese, Barak
title: Watermarks in the Sand: Impossibility of Strong Watermarking for Language Models
claim: strong watermarks are impossible, even with a secret key
realization: attacker with a quality oracle and a perturbation oracle random-walks over good outputs until the mark is gone; mixing-time analysis

title: Proofs of Ownership for Machine Learning Models
claim: ownership of a black-box classifier class is provable exactly when the class is not self-correctable
realization: dichotomy theorem under standard cryptographic assumptions (abstract only)

title: SoK: Watermarking for AI-Generated Content
claim: systematization of watermark definitions: distortion, computational undetectability, robustness, unforgeability
realization: definitional survey

title: Interactive Proofs for Verifying Machine Learning
claim: a verifier can check an untrusted learner's hypothesis, sometimes with far fewer samples than learning
realization: interactive proofs; for Fourier-sparse functions the prover uses membership queries, the verifier random samples

authors: Gur, Jahanara, Khodabandeh, Rajgopal, Salamatian, Shinkar
title: On the Power of Interactive Proofs for Learning
claim: doubly efficient interactive proofs for agnostic PAC learning
realization: (abstract only)

authors: Jia, Yaghini, Choquette-Choo, Dullerud, Thudi, Chandrasekaran, Papernot
title: Proof-of-Learning: Definitions and Practice
claim: a trainer proves it trained, on the premise that forging costs at least training (premise stated, not proved)
realization: the proof is the training trajectory; the verifier re-executes the largest updates

authors: Fang, Jia, Thudi, Yaghini, Choquette-Choo, Dullerud, Chandrasekaran, Papernot
title: Proof-of-Learning is Currently More Broken Than You Think
claim: proof-of-learning as specified can be forged cheaply
realization: two attacks that pass the spot checks; empirical

title: Publicly-Verifiable Certificates for Statistical Algorithms
claim: a statistical algorithm can publish a validity certificate any verifier checks with few samples
realization: certificates for SQ algorithms; the bound is on the verifier, the prover is unrestricted

title: Robust Traceability from Trace Amounts
claim: accurate high-dimensional marginals reveal who was in the data
realization: fingerprinting-style correlation test with a tight dimension threshold

title: The Sample Complexity of Membership Inference and Privacy Auditing
claim: a membership attacker can need many more samples than the trainer
realization: Gaussian mean estimation with unknown covariance; second-moment lower bound; gap vanishes when the covariance is known

title: White-box vs Black-box: Bayes Optimal Strategies for Membership Inference
claim: under a Gibbs-posterior model of training, the Bayes-optimal membership attack reads the weights only through the loss, so white-box gains nothing over loss-only black-box
realization: Bayes rule applied to a Gibbs posterior over parameters

title: Revealing Information while Preserving Privacy
claim: answers with too little noise reveal the database, at a threshold set by the attacker's compute
realization: linear program plus rounding (polynomial time); exhaustive search (exponential time)

title: Cryptanalytic Extraction of Neural Network Models
claim: a black-box ReLU network's weights can be recovered up to functional equivalence
realization: differential attack at critical points, layer by layer

authors: Canales-Martinez, Chavez-Saab, Hambitzer, Rodriguez-Henriquez, Satpute, Shamir
title: Polynomial Time Cryptanalytic Extraction of Neural Network Models
claim: that extraction runs in polynomial time
realization: three polynomial-time sign-recovery methods

title: Adversarial Examples from Computational Constraints
claim: robust classifiers can exist yet be infeasible to learn
realization: hidden-subspace Gaussian construction with an SQ lower bound

title: Computational Limitations in Robust Classification and Win-Win Results
claim: if robust classifiers exist but are hard to learn, one-way functions exist
realization: constructions under average-case hardness, OWF or LPN, plus the converse reduction

authors: Barak, Goldreich, Impagliazzo, Rudich, Sahai, Vadhan, Yang
title: On the (Im)possibility of Obfuscating Programs
claim: some function families have code that reveals a secret no efficient algorithm with oracle access learns, so virtual black-box obfuscation is impossible in general
realization: unobfuscatable function families built from a secret that the code exposes and oracle access hides
